description: ODC (EDIT and REFACTORING coverage for a block event): touch the contract of an IBlockEvent that THIS job did not create. The base is job:block-events, so the block WfRatingPicker, the event OnRate, the ITriggerNode that fires it and the screen WfRatingDemo with the instance wired by visual authoring already exist when the first op runs - there is not a single model-birth op here, on purpose: creating and editing in the same job proves no maintenance. (1) ADDING A PARAMETER to the already-consumed event is the central question, and the job reads BOTH sides at the same instant to answer it: the ITriggerNode gains, by itself, a third EMPTY IArgument - and without filling it the module fails with ArgumentRequiredExpression -, while the IEventHandler of the instance keeps the SAME key and the SAME two arguments. The reason lies in what each side mirrors: the arguments of the PRODUCER are the parameters of the EVENT, and so the contract rules them; the arguments of the CONSUMER are the INPUTS of the handler action, and so widening the event does not touch them. This is what the guide means by 'changing the contract breaks whoever FIRES and not whoever consumes' - the consumer only moves if it WANTS to, and here it does: it starts reading the new parameter inside the expression of an argument that already existed. (2) SWITCHING IsMandatory from True to False, measured on a witness instance WITHOUT a handler created on purpose: while the inherited True held, that instance was a Verify error (EventHandlerRequiredAction, charged per INSTANCE - block-events-mandatory.json proves it); and the module closing valid with it in there is what proves that the write got in. (3) REFACTORING by rename the two neighbours of the contract, with the consumers linked: the node that fires (RaiseOnRate -> RaiseRating) and the action that consumes (WfRateReceived -> WfRatingCaptured). Both follow by KEY and no consumer needs correction; what does NOT follow is the `@OnRate="WfRateReceived"` written in tests/html/visual/block-event.html, because the fragment lives OUTSIDE the model and visual authoring links by NAME - reapplying it today would no longer find the action. The IBlockEvent itself is NOT renamed here: in this run the `rename` of an IBlockEvent returns success (from/to/consumers) and writes NOTHING, and a job that included it would deliver a false proof; the path is what the file leaves proven on the two neighbours, and the difference is reported to whoever maintains the kernel. Outside the job that declared them there are no aliases: the block and the screen are cited as 'IMobileBlock:Name' and 'IMobileScreen:Name', and a child by the path. Each change has its get BEFORE and its get AFTER, and at the end the things this job did NOT touch are also read.

ops.name: OnRate
ops._why: (0) the starting point is INHERITED: the event already exists before the first op of this job, and came from job:block-events
(1) BEFORE, the contract: InputParameters 2 (Rating, Comment), IsMandatory True and the Description that the other job wrote. It is this object, with this key, that changes 1 and 2 will hit
(2) BEFORE, WHO FIRES: the inherited ITriggerNode, with Arguments 2 and the Event pointing to the key of the event
(3) BEFORE, WHO CONSUMES: the IEventHandler that visual authoring created, with Arguments 2. Keep the key: it has to be the SAME in the gets (6d), (6i) and (9d)
(4) BEFORE: 2 real consumers, one ITriggerNode and one IEventHandler, and none derived
(5) BEFORE, the tree of the producer: the IBlockEvent with two IInputParameter and the ITriggerNode with two IArgument. It is the snapshot the dump (14) is compared with

ops.name: WfSource
ops._why: (6a) CHANGE 1 - adding a parameter to an ALREADY CONSUMED contract. The parent is not a $alias: aliases are local to the job that declares them, and the one who declared this event was another job; outside it the stable reference is the path 'IMobileBlock:WfRatingPicker/OnRate'. The name carries the Wf prefix because the parameter is BORN here - unlike the renames of change 3, which follow the convention of what was already written

ops.value: De onde veio a nota. Acrescentado por block-event-lifecycle.json, DEPOIS de o evento ter consumidores.

ops._why: (6b) AFTER, WHO FIRES - AND THIS IS THE CENTRAL PROOF: compare with the get (2). Arguments went from 2 to 3 without anyone creating the third. The arguments of the ITriggerNode mirror the parameters of the EVENT, so the contract rules them and the platform rebuilds the list by itself

(6c) the new argument, from inside: it exists and is EMPTY. Leaving it that way is delivering an invalid module - the Verify refuses with ArgumentRequiredExpression on this node. That is why 'adding a parameter' is, in practice, a change on the PRODUCER

(6d) AFTER, WHO CONSUMES, at the SAME instant: compare with the get (3). SAME key, SAME Arguments 2, nothing to fill. These arguments mirror the INPUTS of the handler action (WfRateReceived, which still declares Rating and Comment) and not the parameters of the event - and that is why widening the contract does not touch them. The pair (6b)+(6d), read at the same instant, IS the answer to the question
(6e) and the consumers are still the same two of the usages (4): widening the contract neither loses nor gains anyone
(6f) MIGRATE WHO FIRES, which is the only MANDATORY migration of this change. The expression runs in the scope of the block, so it sees the Caption input of the block itself
(6g) AFTER: the same argument as in the get (6c), now with text. It is only from here that the module is deliverable again

(6h) MIGRATE WHO CONSUMES - OPTIONAL, and that is the point. The consumer had nothing to fill; it is touched because the author WANTS to use the new parameter. The path '<instance>/<Event>/<Input>' addresses the argument by the name of the INPUT of the handler (Comment), and the expression runs in a combined scope: Comment and WfSource come from the event, and if needed the variables of the screen would also be seen
(6i) the consumer AFTER choosing to change: the key is the same as in the gets (3) and (6d), there are still 2 arguments, and what changed was the TEXT of one of them

ops.name: WfRatingEcho
ops._why: (7a) CHANGE 2 - the WITNESS, created BEFORE the change so that it can be measured. A second instance of the inherited block, WITHOUT a handler linked. While the inherited IsMandatory is True this instance is a Verify error (EventHandlerRequiredAction, charged per instance - block-events-mandatory.json proves it with two instances and two errors)
the Caption input of the block is still mandatory: what this change will relax is the EVENT, not the parameter
(7b) BEFORE change 2: IsMandatory still True, and InputParameters already 3, which is change 1 showing up here too
(7c) switch the mandatoriness of an INHERITED event. The value being switched was chosen by the other job, at birth; it is the kind of change that only a maintenance job can show

(7d) AFTER: compare with the get (7b). IsMandatory CHANGED (True -> False); Name, the inherited Description and the 3 InputParameters STAYED. And the module closing VALID with the witness of (7a) in there is what proves that this write got in - without it, switching IsMandatory would not have a single observable consequence

(7e) the witness from inside: the IEventHandler is BORN with the instance even if empty - it has Event, it has no Handler. That is why it already counts as a consumer in the usages (8) without ever having been linked to anything
(8) 3 consumers: the ITriggerNode and TWO IEventHandler, one linked and one empty. Compare with the usages (4) and with (6e)

ops.name: RaiseRating
ops._why: (9a) CHANGE 3 - refactor the side of WHO FIRES, with the consumer linked. No Wf prefix on purpose: rename follows the convention of what already existed, and the prefix is for what is BORN in this job, like the WfSource of (6a) and the WfRatingEcho of (7a). It returns consumers=1 and expressionsRewritten=0: the zero is honest, because no inherited expression reads the output of this node - an ITriggerNode has no output

(9b) AFTER: the name is different, the Key is the SAME as in the get (6b), and the Event still points to the key of the event. Renaming the node that fires does not disconnect the firing, and the three arguments (with the WfSource already filled) stay where they were
(9c) the SAME three consumers of the usages (8): the event did not even notice the rename of the node that fires it, because the link is by key

ops.name: WfRatingCaptured
ops._why: (10a) refactor the side of WHO CONSUMES, also with the consumer linked: the inherited handler action is now called by what it does. It keeps the Wf prefix because it already carried it from the base. It returns consumers=1, which is the IEventHandler of the instance RatingPicker1

(10b) WHAT FOLLOWED: the consumer has the SAME key as in the get (3), and the Handler points to the SAME key of the action - it was its name that changed, not the object. This IEventHandler went through change 1 and change 3 without a single hand correction
(10c) by the NEW name, the same single consumer: the rename relinks by key and loses no one

ops.name: WfRateReceived
ops._why: (10d) empty list: the old name disappeared from the module. Note what THIS does not say - the `@OnRate="WfRateReceived"` written in tests/html/visual/block-event.html is still there, because the fragment is a file OUTSIDE the model; visual authoring links by NAME, so reapplying that fragment today would no longer find the action

ops.value: Bloco de avaliacao. Contrato mantido por block-event-lifecycle.json: OnRate ganhou o parametro WfSource e deixou de ser obrigatorio.
ops._why: (11) document the maintenance in the inherited block itself, which until now had an empty Description. An IMobileBlock is a TOP-LEVEL NAMED element: the data contract stores this write by the key of the block and will read it back at the end, as it does for an entity - if it did not take effect, the job would fail with Data property mismatch even with a clean Verify

ops.value: Handler da instancia RatingPicker1. Nao foi preciso mexer-lhe quando o evento ganhou o terceiro parametro; so o texto de um argumento passou a citar WfSource.
ops._why: the same on the consuming action, now by the new name: an IScreenAction is also a top-level named element and is also checked at the end

(12) WHAT STAYED: the inherited handler action, with the SAME two InputParameters (Rating, Comment) it was born with. Widening the contract of the event to three parameters did not add any to it - whoever wants the third reads it in the expression of the argument, as (6h) did
(13) WHAT STAYED: the inherited screen action that fires, with the same 4 nodes. Changing the contract of the event does not rewrite the flow, only the argument list of one of its nodes

(14) WHAT STAYED: an inherited parameter of the event that this job did not touch - Integer and with no Description, to be seen side by side with the WfSource of (6a), which was born here with a type and author text

(15) the final tree of the producer, next to the dump (5): the WfSource enters at the END of the parameter sequence of the event and the two inherited ones keep their birth order; the node that fires is now called RaiseRating and has three IArgument, the third with text

(16) the final tree of the consumer: the instance RatingPicker1 of the fragment is still exactly where it was, with its two-argument IEventHandler, and the WfRatingEcho enters beside it, with an empty IEventHandler that is no longer an error today
